title: Installing the Angular CLI and Creating an App
summary: Install Node.js and the Angular CLI, create a project with ng new, run it with ng serve, understand the generated files and generate your first component.
introduction: Angular code has to be compiled before a browser can run it, and the Angular CLI is the tool that does the compiling, serving, testing and building. In this lesson you install it, create a project, start the development server and look at every file the CLI generated so that nothing in the project is a mystery. By the end you will have a running app that reloads the browser each time you save.
learningObjectives: Install Node.js and the Angular CLI and verify the versions
Create and run a new Angular 22 project with ng new and ng serve
Explain the purpose of each generated file and generate a component with ng generate

blocks.text: Angular's tooling runs on [Node.js](/tutorials/nodejs). Install the current long-term-support line (Node.js 24) from nodejs.org, open a terminal and check that `node` and `npm` answer. Your patch versions will differ from the ones shown.
Next install the Angular CLI globally so that the `ng` command is available in every folder. Pinning the major version keeps you on Angular 22 even after Angular 23 is released.

Create a project with ng new

`ng new` creates a folder, writes the configuration, installs the dependencies and initialises a Git repository. It asks a few questions first; the defaults are fine for this tutorial. Newer CLI versions may add a question or two, for example about generating configuration files for AI coding tools, and the defaults are fine there as well.

blocks.text: Open `http://localhost:4200` and you will see the CLI's welcome page. Leave `ng serve` running: every time you save a file it recompiles in well under a second and the browser updates itself. `npm start` runs the same command, so either works.

blocks.title: Common mistake: running ng commands in the wrong folder
blocks.text: `ng serve`, `ng generate`, `ng test` and `ng build` only work inside a project folder, where `angular.json` lives. Run them one level up and you get `The serve command requires to be run in an Angular project, but a project definition could not be found.` Check the terminal's current folder before assuming the installation is broken.

blocks.text: Angular 20 changed the naming convention: files are called `app.ts` rather than `app.component.ts` and classes are called `App` rather than `AppComponent`. Older projects and tutorials still use the suffixes; both styles work, but new projects follow the shorter one.

src/app/app.config.ts (generated)

blocks.text: Notice what is missing: there is no `zone.js` in the dependencies and no zone provider in the configuration. New Angular 22 projects are zoneless; the [signals lesson](/tutorials/angular/signals) explains how change detection works without it. Depending on the exact CLI version you may also see an explicit `provideZonelessChangeDetection()` in the list, which has the same effect.
The generated `app.html` is a long welcome page. Replace its entire content with two lines, save, and watch the browser update.
You could create component files by hand, but `ng generate` writes the class, template, stylesheet and a test in one go, with the naming conventions already applied. `ng g c` is the short form.

blocks.text: The generated class is `Greeting` with the selector `app-greeting`. The `app-` prefix is the project's default and avoids clashes with native and third-party elements. Useful flags: `--inline-template` and `--inline-style` keep everything in the `.ts` file for small components, and `--skip-tests` omits the spec file. The [components lesson](/tutorials/angular/components) explains what to put inside.

blocks.title: Editor support
blocks.text: Install the Angular Language Service extension for [VS Code](/tutorials/vscode). It checks templates as you type, autocompletes component selectors and inputs, and jumps from a tag in a template to the component class.
